question: For good body position, the manual says you should sit so you use your arms to:
choice_a: Brace against the tank during acceleration
choice_b: Steer the motorcycle rather than hold yourself up
choice_c: Signal to other riders in a group
explanation: Sit so you can use your arms to steer the motorcycle rather than to hold yourself up.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: Sitting far enough forward that your arms are slightly bent when holding the handgrips allows you to:
choice_a: Reach the ground more easily at stops
choice_c: Press on the handlebars without having to stretch
choice_d: Shift gears with less clutch travel
explanation: Sit far enough forward so that your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handlegrips; bending your arms permits you to press on the handlebars without having to stretch.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: The manual recommends starting with your right wrist flat on the throttle because it helps you:
choice_a: Grip the front brake lever more firmly
choice_d: Keep from accidentally using too much throttle
explanation: Start with your right wrist flat; this will help you keep from accidentally using too much throttle.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: Keeping your knees against the gas tank while riding helps you:
choice_a: Keep your balance as the motorcycle turns
explanation: Keep your knees against the gas tank to help you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: According to the manual, why should you keep your feet firmly on the footpegs rather than letting them drag?
choice_b: A dragging foot that catches on something can injure you and affect your control of the motorcycle
choice_c: It wears out your boots faster
choice_d: It reduces the effectiveness of the rear brake
explanation: Keep your feet firmly on the footpegs to maintain balance. Don't drag your feet -- if your foot catches on something, you can be injured and it could affect your control of the motorcycle.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Body Position'

question: Why does the manual say to remain in first gear while stopped in traffic?
choice_a: It keeps the engine cooler at idle
choice_b: It is required by Pennsylvania law
choice_c: So you can move out quickly if you need to
choice_d: It prevents the clutch from wearing out
explanation: Shift down through the gears with the clutch as you slow or stop, and remain in first gear while you are stopped so that you can move out quickly if you need to.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Shifting Gears'

question: What can happen if you shift into a lower gear without riding slowly enough first?
choice_a: The engine will stall immediately every time
choice_b: The front brake will lock automatically
choice_d: The motorcycle will lurch, and the rear wheel may skid
explanation: Make certain you are riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear. If not, the motorcycle will lurch, and the rear wheel may skid.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Shifting Gears'

question: If you must shift gears while already in a turn, the manual says you should:
choice_a: Shift smoothly, since a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid
choice_b: Pull in the clutch and coast through the rest of the turn
choice_c: Shift as quickly as possible to minimize time off-throttle
choice_d: Avoid using the clutch at all
explanation: It is best to change gears before entering a turn; however, if shifting while in the turn is necessary, do so smoothly -- a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.9, 'Shifting Gears'

question: About how much of a motorcycle's total stopping power can the front brake provide?
choice_b: At least three-quarters, or 70% or more
choice_c: Roughly half, equal to the rear brake
choice_d: None -- the rear brake does almost all the stopping
explanation: The front brake is more powerful and can provide at least three-quarters of total stopping power; elsewhere the manual states the front brake can provide 70% or more of potential stopping power. The front brake is safe to use if used properly.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.10 and p.23, 'Braking' / 'Quick Stops'

question: Why does the manual recommend using both brakes every time you slow or stop, even for normal stops?
choice_a: Pennsylvania law requires both brakes to be applied simultaneously at all times
choice_b: Using only one brake damages the tires faster
choice_c: It develops the proper habit and skill for using both brakes correctly in an emergency
choice_d: It extends the life of the front brake pads
explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow or stop. Using both brakes for even 'normal' stops will permit you to develop the proper habit or skill of using both brakes properly in an emergency.

question: What does the manual warn can happen if you grab at the front brake or jam down on the rear brake?
choice_c: Nothing, as long as you are riding in a straight line
choice_d: The brakes can lock, resulting in control problems
explanation: Squeeze the front brake and press down on the rear. Grabbing at the front brake or jamming down on the rear can cause the brakes to lock, resulting in control problems.

question: According to the manual, why does leaning a motorcycle in a turn reduce the amount of braking you can safely apply?
choice_a: Some of the traction is used for cornering, leaving less traction available for stopping
choice_b: The front brake disconnects automatically while leaned
choice_c: Leaning increases stopping distance regardless of braking
choice_d: The rear brake becomes the only usable brake while leaned
explanation: When leaning the motorcycle some of the traction is used for cornering. Less traction is available for stopping. A skid can occur if you apply too much brake.

question: In the manual's four-step turning sequence (Slow, Look, Press, Roll), what does the 'Look' step involve?
choice_a: Watching the center line closely for the entire turn
choice_b: Looking through the turn to where you want to go, turning your head (not your shoulders) with eyes level with the horizon
choice_c: Checking your mirrors instead of looking ahead
choice_d: Looking down at the front wheel to judge lean angle
explanation: LOOK -- Look through the turn to where you want to go. Turn just your head, not your shoulders, and keep your eyes level with the horizon.

question: To turn left, the manual says you should press on the:
choice_a: Right handgrip, which leans the motorcycle left
choice_c: Left handgrip, which leans the motorcycle left
choice_d: Front brake lever while looking left
explanation: To turn, the motorcycle must lean. Press on the handgrip in the direction of the turn: press left handgrip -- lean left -- go left.

question: In the 'Roll' step of a turn, rolling on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed serves to:
choice_a: Reduce the lean angle to zero
explanation: ROLL -- Roll on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed. This helps stabilize the motorcycle.

question: In a normal turn, how should the rider and motorcycle lean relative to each other?
choice_a: Only the motorcycle should lean; the rider stays upright
choice_b: Both should lean together at the same angle
choice_c: Only the rider should lean; the motorcycle stays upright
choice_d: The rider should lean opposite the motorcycle
explanation: In normal turns, the rider and the motorcycle should lean together at the same angle.

question: In slow, tight turns, the manual recommends counterbalancing by:
choice_a: Leaning your body more than the motorcycle
choice_b: Leaning both body and motorcycle together at a steep angle
choice_c: Leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body straight
choice_d: Keeping both the body and motorcycle perfectly upright
explanation: In slow, tight turns, counterbalance by leaning the motorcycle only and keeping your body straight.

question: The manual notes that some motorcycles have integrated braking systems that link the front and rear brakes together by:
choice_a: Applying the front brake lever only
choice_b: Turning the ignition key to a special position
explanation: Some motorcycles have integrated braking systems that link the front and rear brakes together by applying the rear brake pedal. Consult the owner's manual for a detailed explanation of these systems.
